title: Why You Can Only See Your Breath in Winter | Why It Happens #10
simplified: Simplified model: the 'water the air can hold' bar is drawn from saturation vapour pressure (Stull table); the line for the breath's water assumes warm breath close to saturation; molecules and droplets are not to scale.

hook_candidates.text: Same breath. So why do you only see it in winter?
Your breath is a cloud. You just can't see it in summer.
You breathe out water every time. Where does it hide?
Watch this bar. When it hits the line, your breath appears.
It's the same breath. Why is only one of them visible?

parts.text: So why do you only see it in winter?
Once this bar drops below the line, you'll see it.
parts.tts: Once this bar drops below the line... you'll see it.

parts.text: Warm air has room for all of it,
and near freezing it holds about a seventh as much.
The extra water squeezes into tiny droplets.
That's a cloud, like the ones in the sky.
parts.tts: That's a cloud! Like the ones in the sky.

sources: Breath carries water vapour that condenses in cold air: 'the water in your moist breath changes from a gas—water vapor—to liquid droplets, which form a fog'; 'When moist air cools off, the water vapor in the air can change from a gas to a liquid, resulting in countless tiny droplets of water.' NSTA Science and Children, Jan 2020, https://www.nsta.org/science-and-children/science-and-children-january-2020/q-why-can-i-see-my-breath-cold-days

Exhaled air is warm and saturated or nearly saturated: 'The expired air was found to be saturated, or very close to saturation, for all conditions studied'; expired air about 28 to 34 C. Cain et al., Defence Research Establishment Ottawa Report 1004 (1989), https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/pdfs/ADA210378.pdf

Cold air holds less water vapour: 'colder air has a smaller capacity for holding water vapor than warmer air'. Saturation vapour pressure over water (Table 4-1): 0 C 0.6113 kPa, 30 C 4.360 kPa, 35 C 5.829 kPa. Stull, Practical Meteorology ch. 4, https://geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Meteorology_and_Climate_Science/Practical_Meteorology_(Stull)/04%3A_Water_Vapor/4.00%3A_Vapor_Pressure_at_Saturation
'About a seventh as much': 0.6113 / 4.360 = 0.14 (1/7.1) against breath at 30 C; against breath at 34-35 C it is about a ninth, so 'about a seventh' is conservative.

Same process as clouds: 'This cloud formation is very similar to the process that occurs when you breath on a cold winter day and you can see your own breath in the form of a cloud.' NWS Flagstaff, Clouds and Contrails, https://www.weather.gov/fgz/cloudscontrails; 'A cloud is essentially a whole lot of fog way up high.' NSTA (above).
